title: Canal, Grid and Clock: Sapporo on the Toyohira Fan
standfirst: Before it was a grid, this ground was a fan of gravel where a shogunate farm dug an irrigation ditch. Judges, an American professor and a beer brewery turned that ditch into a capital's spine. This dossier follows the canal, the firebreak and the bell tower from 1857 to the park that reopened above the river in 2011.

paragraphs.text: Sapporo's city government offers two explanations for its own name and says both are right. Where the Toyohira River spreads its gravel across open ground, the Ainu called the place sat poro, "the dry, vast place"; where the same river's lower course meets the Ishikari River in reed and marsh, it was sari poro pet, "the place of the great wetland." The upper fan is genuinely dry, the lower stretch genuinely wet, and the modern grid sits on the fan, on ground the Toyohira River built by dropping its gravel as it slowed onto the plain.

How long people lived on that fan before anyone wrote it down, Sapporo's own 1911 district history could not say: it records scattered Ainu villages and stone tools turned up by later farmers, and leaves their age open. What it dates precisely is the moment officialdom first marked the ground for settlement: the twenty-fourth day of the second month of Ansei 4, 1857, when the Hakodate magistrate Muragaki Awaji-no-kami Norimasa set aside Sapporo's forest for shogunate retainers, opened a road toward Chitose and sent farmers to nearby Hassamu. When a Colonization Commission judge finally rode in twelve years later, he found the site empty but for two men, ferrymen named Shinmura Tetsuichi and Yoshida Mohachi, camped by the Toyohira crossing since the 1850s.

sections.heading: A Shogunate Farm and the Ditch That Outlasted It

paragraphs.text: The first person to build anything permanent on this ground was not a Colonization Commission official but a shogunate land agent, Ōtomo Kametarō (大友亀太郎), who worked by the agronomist Ninomiya Sontoku's methods. Ordered by the Hakodate magistrate to develop land near Sapporo, he explored the area with a local guide in 1866 and chose a plain thick with oak trees at what is now Higashi Ward's Motomura, close enough to the Toyohira River for irrigation and firm enough underfoot to build on. He brought in farming households ten at a time, cleared more than forty chō of fields in three years, and by his own account governed his settlers strictly but excused their taxes for a decade.

To water his fields and his settlers, Ōtomo hired a foreman named Kurotaki Daijirō and dug an irrigation channel now known as Ōtomo-bori (大友堀): about half a metre deep and six shaku — some 1.8 metres — wide at the top, narrowing toward the bed, running from near today's Minami 3-jō north to Minami 6-jō before bending away to the Fushiko River. The work took only months. After the Meiji Restoration, Ōtomo handed his post to a War Ministry official and left for Tōbetsu; but his ditch stayed in the ground, and its north-south line — not any survey the new government later commissioned — became the axis the whole future city was built along.

Officialdom arrived in earnest in November 1869. Judge Shima Yoshitake (島義勇) rode in from a temporary office at Zenibako, staked out the town's ropes on the eleventh and twelfth of that month at what is now south of Ōdori, and put up the settlement's first government building on the Sosei riverside, near today's Toyohira-kan site, using Nanbu-region carpenters and Zenibako fishermen he pressed into service when local labour ran out. Snow buried each day's work by the next morning; his men laid straw mats to protect the timbers and stripped elm bark to feed the horses when fodder ran short. Shima's own tenure lasted only three months, but Sapporo's district history credits him with the bold, oversized plan that his successors had no choice but to fill: town blocks three chō square, main roads three ken wide.

Shima's Sapporo also collided with the War Ministry, which controlled the neighbouring Ishikari district and had its own plan for the newly surrendered Aizu domain: by October 1869 it had already shipped some two hundred households, more than seven hundred people, to Otaru, intending to settle them at Sapporo itself. When the Colonization Commission's jurisdiction prevailed instead, the War Ministry redirected its Aizu settlers to found Tōbetsu, a little to the north — one of several quiet decisions that shaped which nearby town absorbed the old regime's defeated retainers and which one became the capital.

Shima's successor, Judge Iwamura Michitoshi (岩村通俊), inherited the ditch as much as the plan. In 1870 an official named Sasaki Kanzō proposed widening Ōtomo's channel for boat traffic rather than digging a new canal from scratch; Iwamura agreed, and workers deepened it north to the Kotoni River confluence and south past Minami 7-jō, a stretch later called Yoshida-bori after its subcontractor — Yoshida Mohachi, the same ferryman Shima had found camping at the Toyohira crossing. Iwamura also surveyed a broad east-west firebreak, twelve ken (about 22 metres) wide, separating the government quarter to its north from the merchants' quarter to its south; renamed for Hokkaido's old provinces in 1872 and stripped of that scheme in 1881, Shiribeshi-dōri became simply Ōdori, the avenue that still divides the city today. The channel itself was renamed the Sosei River in 1874.

sections.heading: An American Professor for a Capital of Farmers

paragraphs.text: Kuroda Kiyotaka, who would come to lead the whole colonisation project, went further than any predecessor to find outside help. He sent seven Japanese students abroad to study, and through the Japanese minister in Washington, Mori Arinori, he recruited Horace Capron, the United States Commissioner of Agriculture and an army major general, as chief foreign adviser. The two men's surviving letters, quoted at length in Sapporo's 1911 history, show Mori laying out Hokkaido's size and resources in careful, formal prose and Capron answering with a list of conditions — an annual salary, an interpreter, a house — before he would agree to come.

Capron's recommendations led, in 1876, to Sapporo Agricultural College, and to the year its own graduates would remember longest. William S. Clark, on leave from the presidency of the Massachusetts Agricultural College, arrived that August with two of his own graduates as junior instructors and stayed only a single year. In that year, by his students' own account, he set the school's tone: he gathered them for Bible readings and prayer every morning although religious instruction was not on the syllabus, over Director Kuroda's objections, and told them bluntly at the opening ceremony that Japan needed capable people and that they, its first class, would have to become them. When he left he is remembered for four words of farewell — "Boys, be ambitious" — which the college kept as its unofficial motto for a century after.

The new capital's spiritual centre moved in step with its physical one. Three guardian deities of colonisation had already been enshrined in Tokyo in September 1869 and carried north by Judges Higashikuze and Shima; after a temporary home near today's Kita 2-jō, the shrine settled permanently at Maruyama in September 1871, took the name Sapporo Shrine that year, and was not renamed Hokkaido Shrine, with the Meiji Emperor added as a fourth deity, until 1964 — a reminder of how gradually a frontier settlement's institutions became a prefecture's, then a nation's.

Through the 1870s and 1880s, government-run enterprises gave the grid its economy. A brewery the Colonization Commission opened on 23 September 1876 — the first full-scale beer brewery in Japan built and run entirely by Japanese hands, according to its own corporate history — became, after later reorganisation, the direct ancestor of today's Sapporo Beer; a hemp and linen mill followed in 1888. A railway guide published in 1938 could still describe the city, by then two hundred thousand strong, as sitting "like a go board" in the plain's south-west corner, its main streets lined with the acacia trees planted in those decades, its brewery and mill still turning out beer, sailcloth and yarn for the whole prefecture.

For visiting dignitaries the Commission built Toyohira-kan (豊平館) in 1880, a wooden Western-style hotel completed that December with a lawn and curved paths laid out in front by the American adviser Louis Boehmer using flowers raised at the Agricultural College's own greenhouse; the Meiji Emperor lodged there during his 1881 tour of Hokkaido, the first of three imperial generations to do so. The same year, in the Agricultural College's drill hall nearby, a pendulum clock ordered from the Boston firm E. Howard & Co. began keeping time for the whole town; the tower still carries it today, and Sapporo made it the city's official standard clock in 1888.

When the college moved to a larger campus in 1903, Sapporo borrowed its old drill hall as a public hall and library, and only then did people start calling the building simply the Clock Tower. A red-brick prefectural office building of 1888, its walls said to hold some two and a half million bricks, rose a few streets away as the same government outgrew its wooden Meiji offices — a second, sturdier landmark for the same young capital.

sections.heading: War at the Edges, a River Rebuilt

paragraphs.text: Sapporo was not a target of the incendiary raids that burned Japan's larger cities, but it was not untouched. On 14 and 15 July 1945, American aircraft strafed and bombed the army airfield at Okadama, an oil depot at Teine-Karugawa — seven tanks burned for three days — and the rail yards at Shiroishi, all on the city's edges rather than in the central grid; the city's own peace archive names one civilian killed in the attacks, a farmer strafed in his fields, and his wounded son.

Sapporo's next transformation came from an Olympics. Chosen to host the Eleventh Winter Games, the city opened its first subway line — the Namboku Line, twelve kilometres from Kita 24-jō to Makomanai — on 16 December 1971, together with an underground shopping street downtown, both built as Olympic infrastructure according to the city's own Olympic museum; the Games' opening ceremony followed on 3 February 1972 at the Makomanai outdoor stadium, before athletes from thirty-five countries. The Games also left central Sapporo a problem it would spend decades solving: a Sosei River now boxed in by a four-lane road and two car underpasses that cut the east side of downtown off from the west.

The fix came in 2011, when the city finished linking those underpasses and returned the surface above them to people rather than cars, opening Sosei River Park along both banks. A neighbourhood association's 1967 monument marking Sapporo's founding site, until then wedged into a building lot nearby, was moved into the new park at the foot of Sosei-bashi — the same bridge Judge Iwamura named in 1871, over the same channel Ōtomo Kametarō had dug as an irrigation ditch a century and a half before.

Stand at the corner of Ōdori and the Sosei River and the whole sequence is underfoot: the firebreak axis running east-west, the canal-turned-river running north-south, exactly where Iwamura's surveyors and Ōtomo's ditch-diggers left them. The Clock Tower, moved a hundred metres south in 1906 for road works but otherwise little changed, still keeps the time its Boston-made pendulum has kept since 1881. A few streets north, the red-brick former government building reopened in July 2025 after roughly five years of restoration, its exhibits now including new digital displays on Ainu culture alongside the colonial-era offices.

Two blocks east, Nijo Market still trades on the site where Ishikari-coast fishermen once tied up their boats on the Sosei's bank to sell the morning's catch; a thirteen-shop fish sellers' union formed there in the Meiji era survived an 1902 fire and grew into the market that still calls itself the city's kitchen. None of the timber buildings of 1869 survive above ground, but the lines they were set out on — the ditch, the firebreak, the three-ken roads — are the lines the modern city still keeps its address grid on.

timeline.what: Hakodate magistrate Muragaki Norimasa sets aside Sapporo's forest for shogunate retainer settlement.
Ōtomo Kametarō settles farming households at Motomura and digs the irrigation channel later called Ōtomo-bori.
The three guardian deities of colonisation are enshrined in Tokyo, the origin of Sapporo (later Hokkaido) Shrine.
Judge Shima Yoshitake begins building the new capital at Sapporo.
The War Ministry, denied jurisdiction over Sapporo, redirects its Aizu-domain settlers to found Tōbetsu instead.
Judge Iwamura Michitoshi surveys the grid and the Ōdori firebreak; Kuroda Kiyotaka travels abroad and hires Horace Capron.
The widened Ōtomo-bori is renamed the Sosei River.
Sapporo Agricultural College opens under William S. Clark; the Colonization Commission's brewery, ancestor of Sapporo Beer, opens on 23 September.
Toyohira-kan is built for state guests; a Boston-made pendulum clock begins ringing in the Agricultural College's drill hall.
The Agricultural College moves; its old drill hall, borrowed by the city, becomes known as the Clock Tower and is later moved 100 m south.
American air raids hit Sapporo's edges at Okadama, Teine and Shiroishi.
The Namboku subway line and an underground mall open for the Winter Olympics, whose opening ceremony is held on 3 February 1972.
Sosei River Park opens above the reconnected underpasses; the 1967 founding monument is moved into it.

walk.name: Sapporo Clock Tower
walk.what: Look up at the pendulum clock, made by Boston's E. Howard & Co. and running since 1881, inside the Agricultural College's 1878 drill hall; displays inside recall its move 100 m south in 1906 and its years as the city's library.

walk.name: Former Hokkaido Government Building (Red Brick)
walk.ja: 北海道庁旧本庁舎（赤れんが庁舎）
walk.what: An 1888 brick office building, reopened in July 2025 after a five-year restoration, with new exhibits on Hokkaido's colonisation, including Ainu culture, alongside the original government rooms.

walk.name: Ōdori Park at the Sosei crossing
walk.ja: 大通公園（創成川通交差点）
walk.what: Stand where Ōdori meets the Sosei River: the east-west line underfoot is Iwamura's 1871 firebreak, the north-south watercourse is Ōtomo Kametarō's 1866 irrigation ditch, enlarged and renamed in 1874.

walk.name: Sosei River Park and the "Sapporo Construction Site" monument
walk.ja: 創成川公園・札幌建設の地碑
walk.what: At the foot of Sosei-bashi, a black granite monument raised by a neighbourhood association in 1967 and moved here when the park opened in 2011 marks where Judge Shima's first government building stood in 1869.

walk.name: Nijo Market
walk.what: A working fish and produce market on the Sosei's east bank, tracing its trade to Meiji-era fishermen who rowed catches up the river, and to a thirteen-shop union formed soon after; rebuilt following an 1902 fire.

deepResearchLeads.how: Search the university archive's manuscript catalogue and request access through its reading room.

deepResearchLeads.how: Request site survey reports (発掘調査報告書) for known sites within the central wards; contact the Ainu and Indigenous Studies Center for published research on the same ground.

caveats: Two official sources give slightly different years for Toyohira-kan's move to Nakajima Park (dismantled in 1957 per one account, "moved in May 1958" per another); this dossier follows both, as dismantled in 1957 and reassembled by 1958.

Ōtomo-bori's original depth is recorded in the 1911 district history in a form of shaku/sun notation that this dossier reads as roughly half a metre; the source is not fully unambiguous on this single figure.
Casualty figures for the July 1945 air raids are incomplete in the sources read here: the city's Peace Virtual Museum names one civilian death, not a comprehensive toll for all three targets.

Pre-1857 Ainu settlement within today's central grid is described only in general terms (scattered villages, stone tools) by the 1911 district history used here; it does not identify exact sites, which would need the archaeological leads listed above.
